sentences.text: This dinosaur reached lengths between 7 and 8.3 meters and had a mass of roughly 2.2 tonnes.
Its head was substantial, measuring exactly 67.0 centimeters from tip to tip.
Although it was a herbivore that primarily walked on two legs, it could also move on four limbs.
The most striking feature was a large structure along its back, held up by very long and wide bony spikes that ran from the hips to the tail.
The name carries a double meaning, combining Arabic words for bravery with the Tuareg name for a desert lizard.
It possessed large, muscular cheeks that acted like a net to keep food from falling out of its mouth.
Spaces between its chewing teeth were filled with the growing tips of replacement teeth, creating a smooth, continuous grinding surface.
Two nearly complete skeletons were found in the Elrhaz Formation in Agadez, Niger, during expeditions in 1965 and 1970.
These remains came from five separate French expeditions led by Philippe Taquet between 1965 and 1972.
The very first team, working in January and February 1965, uncovered eight specimens of this group at a site called the niveau des Innocents.
The genus was officially named in 1976 by the French paleontologist Philippe Taquet.
The muscles controlling its jaws were relatively weak.
Despite this, it likely used its teeth to chew tough and hard plant materials.
Bone tissue showing signs of rapid repair and high blood vessel density suggests this individual grew very quickly.
The structure of its legs indicates they functioned as sturdy pillars for support rather than for fast running.
A four-legged stance would have been physically possible for the animal.
Scientists usually explain the back structure as a system for regulating body temperature or a tool for visual display.
However, a recent study from 2026 argues that this dinosaur was likely an obligate quadruped, meaning it almost always walked on four legs.
It was first placed in the family Iguanodontidae in 1976, but this group is now considered paraphyletic and is no longer used in classification.
Its parent group is identified as Neoiguanodontia.
It is placed within the clade Hadrosauroidea, which includes the famous duck-billed dinosaurs and their close relatives.
This animal lived during the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 110 million years ago, in what is now Africa.
Fossils are known from the Elrhaz Formation of the Tegama Group in the Gadoufaoua area of Niger.
It inhabited the upper portion of the Elrhaz Formation, which is probably of Aptian age.
Its time range extends from the Aptian to the Maastrichtian stages, spanning from 121.4 to 66 million years ago.
It is debated whether the back carried a sail or a hump of muscle tissue or fat similar to a bison or camel.
The phylogenetic relationships of Ouranosaurus remained uncertain for decades after its description.
